desc:
The array costs lists the hiring cost of the workers standing in a queue, costs[i] being the cost of the worker at position i. You must run exactly k hiring rounds. In each round:

  • look only at the first candidates workers and the last candidates workers of the workers still waiting (if fewer than 2 * candidates are waiting, all of them are visible; nobody is counted twice);
  • hire the visible worker with the lowest cost; if several have that cost, take the one with the smallest original index.

A hired worker leaves the queue and the others keep their order. Return the total cost of the k hired workers.

costs = [17, 12, 10, 2, 7, 2, 11, 20, 8], k = 3, candidates = 4
round 1: visible 17 12 10 2 | 2 11 20 8 -> hire index 3 (cost 2)
round 2: visible 17 12 10 7 | 2 11 20 8 -> hire index 5 (cost 2)
round 3: visible 17 12 10 7 | 7 11 20 8 -> hire index 4 (cost 7)
total = 11
hints: A direct simulation scans the visible workers in every round. That is O(k * candidates). Can you find the cheapest visible worker faster?
The visible workers form two groups: the front group and the back group. Keep each group in its own min-heap of (cost, index).
After hiring from a group, slide the window: take the next waiting worker from that side (the front pointer moves right, the back pointer moves left) as long as the two pointers have not crossed.
editorial: Maintain two pointers l and r that delimit the workers not yet shown to any heap. First push the first candidates workers into a left min-heap and the last candidates workers into a right min-heap, never pushing a worker that was already pushed (stop when l > r).

In each round compare the tops of the two heaps as (cost, index) pairs. Because every index in the left heap is smaller than every index in the right heap, comparing the pairs directly gives the right tie-break. Pop the better one, add its cost, and refill the heap it came from with the next unseen worker on that side if one is left.
Every worker enters a heap at most once and each round performs O(1) heap operations, so the total time is O((candidates + k) log candidates) and the memory is O(candidates).
